\chapter{Estudiante --- a Word You Can Build}
\label{ch:estudiante}
\hlchaptermodality{52}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can build a person-word from a verb with -ante, and read it as English -ant.}

I can build a person-word from a verb with -ante, and read it as English -ant.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[estudiante]{estudiante}

\label{lesson:ES-C09-estudiante}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}to study.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Estudiar}.) You have had it since your first handful of verbs.

Say \textquotedblleft{}I am a teacher.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Soy profesor} — no \emph{un}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the one who is doing it}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Verb + \emph{-ante} = the person doing it.}
\end{quote}

Take \emph{estudiar}, cut the \emph{-ar}, add \emph{-ante}:

\begin{quote}
\emph{estudi\textbf{ar}} $\to$ \emph{estudi\textbf{ante}} — \textbf{the one who is studying}
\end{quote}

You did not memorise that word. You \textbf{built} it, from a verb you already had.

English uses the same ending, worn down to \emph{-ant}: a \textbf{particip\emph{ant}} takes part, an \textbf{assist\emph{ant}} assists, an \textbf{inhabit\emph{ant}} inhabits. So \emph{-ante} and \emph{-ant} are one more pair for your decoder.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\emph{estudiante} & \textbf{student} \\
\emph{importante} & \textbf{important} \\
\emph{elegante} & \textbf{elegant} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

And \emph{estudiante} also begins \emph{es-} + consonant. Take the \emph{e-} off: \textbf{st}udiante. \textbf{Student}. Two of your rules on one word.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one word, either person}]
\emph{Profesor} changed to \emph{profesora} for a woman. \emph{Estudiante} does not change at all:

\begin{quote}
\emph{Él es estudiante.}  ·  \emph{Ella es estudiante.}
\end{quote}

The article moves instead — \emph{el estudiante}, \emph{la estudiante} — but the word itself stays put. Words ending in \emph{-ante} almost never shift.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Soy estudiante}
  \item \emph{Somos estudiantes}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{-ante} do to a verb? (Makes \textbf{the one doing it}.)

And does \emph{estudiante} change for a woman? (\textbf{No} — only the article does.)
\end{tcolorbox}
